questions.stem: Sasha, 15, is on the ward recovering from DKA and is now alert. Her mother has told you that Sasha's sister says she has been skipping insulin to lose weight. You want to explore this and her wider wellbeing before discharge planning. What is the best way to start this conversation?
options: See Sasha alone, explain confidentiality and its limits, then do a HEEADSSS assessment
Interview Sasha with her mother present so that the history can be corroborated
Open by asking Sasha directly why she has been skipping her insulin to lose weight
Give her a written eating disorder questionnaire to fill in before any interview
questions.why: Adolescents disclose sensitive issues such as disordered eating, mood, alcohol and self-harm much more readily when seen alone, after being told what stays confidential and when you would have to share (risk of serious harm). HEEADSSS gives a structured, non-judgemental way into these topics.
notes: With her mother present, Sasha is less likely to talk openly about weight, mood, alcohol or conflict at home, so parents should be asked to step out for part of the consultation.
Opening with a confronting, blaming question about the sister's report before building rapport and covering confidentiality is likely to make her defensive and shut the conversation down.
A screening tool can help later, but it does not replace a confidential face-to-face psychosocial assessment, and handing it over before any interview damages rapport.

questions.stem: Sasha, 15, has moderate DKA (pH 7.25, HCO3 9 mmol/L, glucose 22 mmol/L, K 4.5 mmol/L) and a GCS of 13. She is not shocked and is passing urine. Rehydration with 0.9% sodium chloride and added potassium has just been started in ED. Following the RCH guideline, how should her insulin be started?
options: IV bolus of 0.1 units/kg, then an infusion at 0.1 units/kg/h started straight away
Subcutaneous NovoMix at her usual dose now, then recheck ketones in 2 hours
IV infusion at 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/h, starting about 1 hour after fluids, with no bolus
IV infusion at 0.1 units/kg/h, started only once the glucose has fallen below 15
questions.why: In paediatric DKA, give an IV insulin infusion at 0.05 to 0.1 units/kg/h about 1 hour after fluids have started, with no bolus. A bolus and early insulin cause a rapid fall in osmolality and are linked to cerebral oedema. Add glucose to the fluids once the BGL is below 15 instead of stopping the insulin.
notes: An insulin bolus is not used in children with DKA. It drops glucose and osmolality too fast and raises the risk of cerebral oedema and hypokalaemia.
Subcutaneous premixed insulin is absorbed unpredictably in a dehydrated, acidotic child and will not reliably switch off ketogenesis. DKA needs an IV infusion.
Insulin is what clears the ketoacidosis, so it must not wait for the glucose to fall. When the BGL drops below 15, glucose is added to the fluids and the insulin continues.

questions.stem: Sasha, 15, with DKA has a plasma potassium of 4.5 mmol/L before treatment. The registrar warns that it will fall once the insulin infusion starts, even though her total-body potassium is already low from vomiting and polyuria. What is the main mechanism of this fall in plasma potassium?
options: Insulin inhibits Na+/K+-ATPase, so potassium leaks out of cells and into the urine
Insulin stimulates Na+/K+-ATPase, shifting potassium from the plasma into cells
Insulin increases aldosterone release, so the kidney secretes more potassium
Saline dilutes plasma potassium, with no real shift of potassium into cells
questions.why: Lack of insulin and high osmolality shift potassium out of cells, while osmotic diuresis and vomiting lose it, so the plasma level looks normal despite a total-body deficit. Insulin switches on Na+/K+-ATPase and drives potassium back into cells. That is why potassium goes into the fluids once K is below 5.5 and she is passing urine.
notes: This is the wrong direction. Insulin stimulates the pump and moves potassium into cells. It does not make it leak out.
Insulin does not meaningfully raise aldosterone. The early fall in potassium happens because potassium moves into cells, not because more is lost through the kidney.
Dilution adds a little, but the main and fastest cause is insulin-driven uptake of potassium into cells. That is why the fall comes when insulin starts.

questions.stem: Six hours into DKA treatment, the nurse calls you about Sasha, 15. She has a new headache, her GCS has fallen to 10, her HR is 58 and her right pupil is dilated and sluggish. You suspect cerebral oedema with transtentorial herniation. Compression of which structure best explains the change in her pupil?
options: Right optic nerve compressed in the optic canal by raised intracranial pressure
Right abducens nerve stretched over the petrous apex of the temporal bone
Right cervical sympathetic chain compressed by displacement of the brainstem
Right oculomotor nerve compressed at the tentorial edge by the herniating uncus
questions.why: In uncal (transtentorial) herniation, the medial temporal lobe presses the oculomotor nerve against the tentorial edge. Its parasympathetic pupillomotor fibres run on the outside of the nerve, so a dilated, sluggish pupil on the same side is an early sign. Neuro obs must include the pupils.
notes: Optic nerve damage causes visual loss and a relative afferent pupillary defect, with both pupils equal in size. It does not cause a single dilated pupil.
Stretching of the abducens nerve is a false localising sign of raised ICP. It weakens the lateral rectus (abduction deficit) and does not change pupil size.
Damage to the sympathetic chain causes Horner syndrome, with a small pupil (miosis) and ptosis, not a dilated one.
